hops.afterHeading: Which neurons die: three diseases, three populations
hops.title: Your big toe versus your eyes in ALS
hops.text: Look from one end of this line to the other, then wiggle your big toe. Both moves ended at lower motor neurons, of very different kinds. Motor neurons in your lower spinal cord send long axons all the way down your leg to the muscles that move your toe. The cells steering your eyes sit in the brainstem, in the oculomotor, trochlear and abducens nuclei, and their short axons reach the eye muscles. In ALS, spinal motor neurons and those that drive speech fail, while the eye-movement neurons hold out late into the disease. That is why patients who can no longer speak can still communicate with eye-tracking computers.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student sitting cross-legged on a sofa reading a book, glancing sideways while wiggling one big toe in a striped sock.
image.caption: Eye-movement motor neurons tend to resist ALS, so eye tracking can help patients keep communicating.

hops.afterHeading: What builds up: proteins that clump
hops.title: Hibernating ground squirrels phosphorylate tau, then reverse it
hops.text: In deep hibernation, Arctic ground squirrels let their body temperature fall to about zero degrees Celsius, and Syrian hamsters in torpor cool to about five. Torpor comes in bouts lasting days, broken by brief rewarmings. During each bout, tau in their neurons picks up extra phosphate groups, the same kind of change found in Alzheimer tangles. In European ground squirrels, phosphorylated tau stains most strongly in the ventral hippocampus, entorhinal cortex and isocortex, while synaptic contacts onto CA3 neurons recede. Researchers found no tau filaments in the tissue they examined. Within hours of rewarming, tau phosphorylation falls and markers of those CA3 synapses begin to recover.

sources.citation: Arendt et al., Journal of Neuroscience 23(18):6972-6981 (2003).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A ground squirrel curled asleep in a grass-lined burrow beneath a snowy winter surface.
image.caption: In hibernating ground squirrels, tau gains phosphates during torpor and starts losing them as the animals warm up.

hops.afterHeading: What can start it: genes that cause and genes that raise risk
hops.title: An Alzheimer risk allele linked to better scores in older Tsimane with high eosinophil counts
hops.text: APOE ε4 is often described as if carrying it sealed a person's fate. It raises the odds of late-onset Alzheimer disease, yet its link to thinking can change with conditions. A study of 372 Tsimane forager-horticulturalists in the Bolivian Amazon asked how APOE ε4 and blood eosinophil counts, an indirect marker of parasitic infection, together relate to cognitive test scores. Among participants aged 45 to 88 with high eosinophil counts, ε4 carriers tended to score higher than non-carriers, whereas at lower counts they scored worse. The authors hypothesize that ε4 may carry an advantage in high-pathogen settings that fades with lower infection exposure.

sources.citation: Trumble et al., The FASEB Journal 31(4):1508-1515 (2017).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A wooden dugout canoe and woven baskets of plantains along a lush sunlit riverbank in the Amazon rainforest.
image.caption: At high blood eosinophil counts, a parasite marker, older Tsimane APOE ε4 carriers tended to score higher than non-carriers.

audio.title: Three puzzles of brain evidence
audio.transcript:
Neurodegeneration has a habit of humbling anyone who jumps straight from a clue to a conclusion. Here are three true stories—one about what builds up, one about what starts it, and one about whether fixing a signal actually helps.

Start in a quiet convent. In the Nun Study, researcher David Snowdon followed six hundred and seventy-eight Catholic sisters from the School Sisters of Notre Dame, aged seventy-five to one hundred and seven. They took annual cognitive and physical tests and agreed to donate their brains after death. One participant, known as Sister Mary, became famous in the study for keeping high cognitive test scores right up to her death at age one hundred and one. When pathologists examined her brain under the microscope, they found abundant amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles—the classic hallmarks of Alzheimer disease. Sister Mary is a reminder of the lesson's first rule: an autopsy tells you what accumulated in the tissue, not by itself whether those deposits stole a person's memory.

Now travel to Colombia, to the world's largest known extended family with dominantly inherited Alzheimer disease. Roughly twelve hundred relatives carry a single mutation in the gene for presenilin one, the catalytic core of the enzyme that makes the second cut in amyloid precursor protein. In that family, carriers typically develop mild cognitive impairment at a median age of forty-four and dementia at forty-nine. Yet one woman carrying the exact same mutation stayed free of mild cognitive impairment until her seventies—nearly three decades past the family's usual onset. When researchers scanned her brain, they found something unexpected. She carried unusually high levels of amyloid plaques, even higher than relatives who had developed memory trouble in their forties. Yet her tau tangles and signs of neurodegeneration were relatively limited, especially for her age. Sequencing showed that she also carried two copies of a rare variant called A P O E three Christchurch. Even a powerful dominant gene and a brain full of amyloid did not, by themselves, decide when her symptoms began.

Finally, jump to cardiology for one of the sharpest lessons in medicine on why a better reading is not a better patient. After a heart attack, frequent extra beats from the heart's lower chambers mark a higher risk of sudden death. Two pills, encainide and flecainide, suppressed those extra beats reliably. Then came the Cardiac Arrhythmia Suppression Trial. Its nineteen ninety-one report on these two drugs covered one thousand four hundred and ninety-eight heart-attack survivors whose extra beats had responded to the pills, each randomly assigned to stay on the drug or switch to placebo. The pills had quieted the extra beats, yet both drug arms had to be stopped early. Over an average of ten months, more than twice as many people died in the drug groups as on placebo, most of them from arrhythmia. Patients assigned to the drugs were less safe, not more, though the investigators noted that the mechanism behind those excess deaths remained unknown.

Put those three stories together and you have the lesson's rule. Plaques at autopsy show what built up. Families show what can start the cascade, and sometimes what can stall it. A randomized trial that measures how people think, function or survive is the most direct test of whether a treatment aimed at a target helps patients.
